title: FALCON: Few-step Accurate Likelihoods for Continuous Flows
claim: A learned flow map transports source samples to a biased target, and self-normalized importance sampling then corrects them to match the true distribution.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right: source-to-target trajectory panel, importance-sampling box, debiased target density, with arrows between stages
description: The figure reads left to right in three stages. On the left, a purple Gaussian-like Source density on a vertical axis sends many faint blue trajectory curves across to a multimodal Biased Target density. A faded outline behind the target marks the True Density. One bold dark-blue trajectory runs from x0 to x1. On it, a red point x_s has a red arrow labeled u_θ(x_s, s, t) pointing to x_t, and small blue arrows labeled v(x_s, s). An arrow then leads to a rounded lavender box titled 'Self-normalized Importance Sampling', which holds the weighted-average formula Σ w(x^k) f(x^k) / Σ w(x^k). A second arrow leads to the Debiased Target density, which closely matches the faint True Density outline. The palette is purple and navy, with red for the flow-map notation. The eye goes first to the dense bundle of trajectories.
caption: Flow map learns from biased data, with SNIS re-weighting generated samples consistent with the Boltzmann distribution, approaching equality with infinite samples under mild regularity conditions.
abstract: Scalable sampling of molecular states in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann Generators tackle this problem by pairing a generative model, capable of exact likelihood computation, with importance sampling to obtain consistent samples under the target distribution. Current Boltzmann Generators primarily use continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) trained with flow matching for efficient training of powerful models. However, likelihood calculation for these models is extremely costly, requiring thousands of function evaluations per sample, severely limiting their adoption. In this work, we propose Few-step Accurate Likelihoods for Continuous Flows (FALCON), a method which allows for few-step sampling with a likelihood accurate enough for importance sampling applications by introducing a hybrid training objective that encourages invertibility. We show FALCON outperforms state-of-the-art normalizing flow models for molecular Boltzmann sampling and is two orders of magnitude faster than the equivalently performing CNF model.
